bigPicture.subtitle: The Cross That Reaches Every Room of Your Life
bigPicture.thesis: If we had to summarize the Book of 1 Corinthians in one overarching thought, it is this: the crucified and risen Christ is not only how you are saved — He is the measure of everything you do with your gifts, your body, your rights, your church and your future, and the way He measures it is love.
paragraphs: Start with the man's name, because he chose it himself. Born Saul, after Israel's tall, impressive first king, he became known in the Gentile world by his Roman name, Paulus — a Latin word that means “small.” Whether or not he picked it for its meaning, he lived it. In this letter he calls himself “the least of the apostles, who is not worthy to be called an apostle” (15:9), arrives in Corinth “in weakness, in fear, and in much trembling” (2:3), and describes himself and his companions as “the filth of the world, the dirt wiped off by all” (4:13). And this small man wrote to the most ambitious city in Greece to tell it that God builds His church out of nobodies, “that no flesh should boast before God” (1:29).

First Corinthians is the most practical book Paul ever wrote, because it was written to a church that had everything and was getting almost everything wrong. They had every spiritual gift (1:7) — and they were splitting into fan clubs behind their favourite preachers. They were proud of their knowledge — and tolerating a sexual sin the pagans would not tolerate. They called each other brothers on Sunday — and sued each other on Monday. They celebrated the Lord's Supper — while the rich got drunk and the poor went home hungry. They spoke in tongues — in a chaos that made visitors think they were mad. And some of them had stopped believing that the dead will rise. It is the portrait of a church that had received grace and was using it to compete.

And Paul's answer to every single problem is the same. He does not give them a better technique. He gives them the cross. “For I determined not to know anything among you, except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (2:2). Factions? “Was Paul crucified for you?” (1:13). Sexual sin? “You were bought with a price” (6:20). Pride in knowledge? “The brother for whose sake Christ died” (8:11). Contempt at the Lord's Table? “You proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes” (11:26). Denial of the resurrection? “If Christ has not been raised, your faith is vain; you are still in your sins” (15:17). Every room in the Corinthians' lives — the meeting hall, the courtroom, the bedroom, the dining room, the temple, the graveyard — gets the same visitor. The cross walks in and rearranges the furniture.

And then, between the chapters on spiritual gifts, Paul writes the chapter the whole world knows — and almost nobody reads in context. First Corinthians 13 is not wedding poetry. It is the scalpel. “If I speak with the languages of men and of angels, but don’t have love, I have become sounding brass, or a clanging cymbal” (13:1). The love Paul describes there — patient, kind, not envious, not proud, not self-seeking, keeping no ledger of wrongs — is the shape of the cross in a human life. It is what Christ is. And it is the one thing that will survive into eternity: “But now faith, hope, and love remain—these three. The greatest of these is love” (13:13). The book ends with the same note, in Paul's own handwriting: “Let all that you do be done in love” (16:14) and “My love to all of you in Christ Jesus” (16:24). Sixteen chapters of correction, and the last word is love.

map.intro: First Corinthians is the seventh book of the New Testament and the second of Paul's letters in the canonical order — placed after Romans, though it was written two or three years before it. The order is not chronological; it is pedagogical. Romans teaches you the gospel. First Corinthians shows you that gospel walking into a real church and dealing with real mess. Here is why it sits where it does:

sections.title: Romans Proclaimed — Corinth Applied
sections.body: Romans is the gospel argued in order: sin, justification, union with Christ, the Spirit, Israel, and then the life of the body (Romans 12–15). First Corinthians takes nearly every one of those doctrines and drops it into a congregation that is failing to live it. Romans 6 says the old self was crucified; 1 Corinthians 6 says “such were some of you, but you were washed” (6:11). Romans 12 says we are one body with differing gifts; 1 Corinthians 12 shows that body arguing about which gift is best. Romans 14 says not to destroy with your food the one for whom Christ died; 1 Corinthians 8 to 10 shows what that means at an actual dinner in a city of temples. If Romans is the blueprint, 1 Corinthians is the building site — with the mud, the noise and the arguments among the builders.

sections.title: The Only Detailed Window Into a First-Century Church
sections.body: No other book of the Bible shows you so much about what early Christian congregations were actually like. Here is the earliest written account of the Lord's Supper (11:23–26), written before any of the Gospels. Here is the oldest creed of the resurrection (15:3–5), handed down within a few years of the event. Here is a picture of worship in which “each one of you has a psalm, has a teaching, has a revelation, has another language, has an interpretation” (14:26). Here is one of the earliest pieces of evidence that believers met on the first day of the week (16:2), and the Aramaic prayer “Maranatha” preserved from the very first church (16:22). Without 1 Corinthians, we would know far less about how the first Christians lived, worshipped, argued and loved.

sections.title: The Resurrection Chapter of the Bible
sections.body: The Old Testament hints at resurrection — Job's “in my flesh shall I see God,” Isaiah 26, Ezekiel's valley of bones, Daniel 12. The Gospels record it. But 1 Corinthians 15 is where Scripture explains it most fully: why it matters (if Christ is not raised, your faith is vain), how it works (Christ the first fruits, then those who are His at His coming), what kind of body it brings (sown perishable, raised imperishable), and what it means for today (your labour is not in vain in the Lord). Paul placed it at the end of the letter on purpose, because every other problem in Corinth — their contempt for the body, their arrogance, their sense that they had already arrived — came from a weak grip on the resurrection. Get the end of the story right, and everything in the middle changes.

roadAhead.intro: The Road Ahead: the next two books continue the story of Paul and his churches, and both take what you have learned here into deeper waters. In 1 Corinthians Paul corrected a church from a position of settled authority, as a father with a rod or with gentleness. In the next letter that authority is under attack, and you will see what it costs him. And in the letter after that, the attack is on the gospel itself.

books.connection: Same church, about a year later — and almost everything has gone wrong. First Corinthians did not fix Corinth. Paul made a painful visit, then wrote a severe letter “out of much affliction and anguish of heart… with many tears” (2 Corinthians 2:4), and rivals arrived who mocked him as weak and unimpressive. In 1 Corinthians Paul taught that God chooses the weak things of the world (1:27) and that he came to them in weakness and trembling (2:3). In 2 Corinthians that theology is tested in his own body. He calls himself a cracked jar: “But we have this treasure in clay vessels, that the exceeding greatness of the power may be of God, and not from ourselves” (2 Corinthians 4:7). He begs three times for a thorn to be removed and receives the answer that completes 1 Corinthians 1: “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9). And the resurrection hope of 1 Corinthians 15 becomes his strength in suffering: “For he was crucified through weakness, yet he lives through the power of God” (2 Corinthians 13:4). Watch, too, for the man disciplined in 1 Corinthians 5 — or perhaps another offender — as Paul pleads for the church to forgive and restore. The father who taught them in the first letter now shows them his scars.

Then the danger moves from behaviour to the gospel itself. In Corinth the problem was a church that took its freedom too far — “All things are lawful for me” — and used it to please itself. In Galatia the problem is the opposite: believers being told that faith in Christ is not enough, that they must also be circumcised and keep the law. Paul's tone is the sharpest in any of his letters: “I marvel that you are so quickly deserting him who called you in the grace of Christ to a different ‘good news’” (Galatians 1:6). And he goes back to the same place he went in Corinth — the cross: “Foolish Galatians, who has bewitched you not to obey the truth, before whose eyes Jesus Christ was openly portrayed among you as crucified?” (Galatians 3:1). Then he holds both errors in a single sentence that 1 Corinthians has prepared you to understand: “For you, brothers, were called for freedom. Only don’t use your freedom for gain to the flesh, but through love be servants to one another” (Galatians 5:13). Corinth abused freedom; Galatia was surrendering it. Both are answered by Christ crucified and by love. You have just spent sixteen chapters learning that freedom exists for love. Galatians will teach you to fight for that freedom.

themesMastered.title: The Cross Ends Every Boast
themesMastered.body: “For the word of the cross is foolishness to those who are dying, but to us who are saved it is the power of God” (1:18). Corinth measured people by eloquence, wisdom, status and success, and it brought those measurements into the church — “I follow Paul,” “I follow Apollos.” Paul answered with the message that offends everyone: a crucified Messiah, a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Greeks, and yet the power and wisdom of God. God deliberately chose the foolish, the weak, the lowly and the despised, “that no flesh should boast before God” (1:29). You now own this truth: in Christ, the ladder of status has been sawn in half. You have nothing you did not receive (4:7). Your preachers belong to you; you belong to Christ (3:21–23). The only boast left is in the Lord.

themesMastered.title: Your Body Belongs to the Lord
themesMastered.body: “Or don’t you know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have from God? You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. Therefore glorify God in your body” (6:19–20). Corinth believed the body did not matter — so some indulged it without limit and others despised it. Paul answered both from the resurrection: “God raised up the Lord, and will also raise us up by his power” (6:14). The body has a future, so what you do with it now matters forever. Sexual immorality is fled, not managed. Marriage is mutual self-giving, not ownership. Freedom is tested by two questions: does it build up, and will it master me? You were bought in the marketplace with the blood of Christ. Your body is now the Holy of Holies.

themesMastered.title: Freedom Is for Love
themesMastered.body: “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up” (8:1). The strong in Corinth were right that idols are nothing — and their correct theology was destroying a weaker brother “for whose sake Christ died” (8:11). Paul showed them a man who had more rights than any of them and refused to use them: “For though I was free from all, I brought myself under bondage to all, that I might gain the more” (9:19). The question is never only, “Am I allowed?” It is, “Will this build up my brother? Will it hinder the gospel? Will it bring me under its power?” And the summary of it all: “Whether therefore you eat, or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God” (10:31). Freedom is not the right to please yourself. It is the power to serve.

themesMastered.title: One Body, Many Gifts — and the Greatest Is Love
themesMastered.body: “Now you are the body of Christ, and members individually” (12:27). Every believer has a gift, given by the Spirit as He wills, for the good of all (12:7, 11). No member can say, “I don’t belong,” and no member can say, “I have no need of you.” God gives more honour to the hidden members, so that the body suffers and rejoices together. And the gifts are measured by love: tongues without love are noise, knowledge without love is nothing, sacrifice without love gains nothing (13:1–3). Love is patient and kind, keeps no ledger of wrongs, and never fails. Prophecy and tongues and knowledge will pass away when we see Him face to face. “But now faith, hope, and love remain—these three. The greatest of these is love” (13:13).

themesMastered.title: The Resurrection Makes Nothing Wasted
themesMastered.body: “Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the Lord’s work, because you know that your labor is not in vain in the Lord” (15:58). Paul staked everything on one historical fact: “that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures” (15:3–4). If not, faith is vain and we are still in our sins. But now Christ has been raised, the first fruits of a guaranteed harvest. Death is the last enemy, and it will be swallowed up in victory. Its sting is gone, because Christ took the sin that gave it power. And because the end of the story is resurrection, every act of faithful love in the middle of the story counts forever.

experientialLesson.intro: How do you walk out the Book of 1 Corinthians practically moving forward? Here is your experiential blueprint:

steps.title: Tear Down the Banner, Take Up the Cross
steps.lesson: The Lesson: “Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you?” (1:13). The first sin Paul confronts in this letter is not immorality but party spirit — believers attaching their identity to human leaders and looking down on others. And his answer is the cross, which flattens every human hierarchy: “God chose the foolish things of the world that he might put to shame those who are wise” (1:27). The church is built from people the world overlooked, so that no one can boast. Everything you are proud of, you received (4:7).
steps.practice: The Practice: This week, do three things. First, name your banner — the leader, church, tradition or style you feel superior about — and confess any contempt you have felt for believers who differ from you. Second, reach out to one believer from a different church or tradition, or someone in your own church you have kept at a distance, and do something to mend the net: a meal, a prayer together, a genuine word of thanks for God's work in them. Third, write down your three greatest strengths, and beside each one write how you received it. Read it aloud and finish with 1:31: “He who boasts, let him boast in the Lord.”

steps.title: Give the Temple Back — and Lay Down a Right
steps.lesson: The Lesson: “You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. Therefore glorify God in your body” (6:19–20). And: “Therefore if food causes my brother to stumble, I will eat no meat forever more” (8:13). Corinth's two great errors were treating the body as unimportant and treating freedom as the right to please oneself. Paul answered both with the cross and the resurrection: your body was purchased and will be raised, and your freedom exists for the sake of your brother and the gospel.
steps.practice: The Practice: Tonight, dedicate your body to God aloud, part by part — eyes, hands, mouth, appetite, sexuality — and name one specific area where you have been treating your body as your own. Decide on one concrete step to flee that temptation within 24 hours: delete the app, end the conversation, change the route, tell a trusted friend. Then choose one freedom you exercise that might cause a weaker believer to stumble, and lay it down for thirty days as an act of love, praying for that person by name every time you miss it. Map your way of escape (10:13) for your most frequent temptation, and take it next time it comes.

steps.title: Do Everything in Love — Because He Is Risen
steps.lesson: The Lesson: “If I speak with the languages of men and of angels, but don’t have love, I have become sounding brass, or a clanging cymbal” (13:1). And: “your labor is not in vain in the Lord” (15:58). The letter ends with “Let all that you do be done in love” (16:14). Every gift, every act of service, every right and every correction must be soaked in the love that is patient, kind, and keeps no record of wrongs. And the resurrection guarantees that not one act of such love will ever be wasted.
steps.practice: The Practice: Read 13:4–7 aloud with your own name in place of “love.” Circle the two lines where your voice catches, and ask the Spirit to grow those fruits in you this month. Name one person you have been keeping a ledger against, and close the account in prayer — tear up the list. Then take the labour for the Lord you are most tempted to give up on, and do one faithful act in it this week, writing the date on a page titled “Seeds Sown.” On the first day of next week, set aside a planned, proportional gift for the Lord's work (16:2). And end each day this week by praying the oldest prayer of the church: Maranatha — Our Lord, come.

finalDeclaration: “Father, I close this letter as a Corinthian who has met the cross. I declare that the word of the cross, which the world calls foolishness, is to me the power of God. I renounce every banner I have carried and every boast I have made. I have nothing that I did not receive. Christ Jesus is my wisdom, my righteousness, my sanctification and my redemption, and I boast in Him alone. I declare that I am Your temple. My body is not my own; I was bought with a price — the precious blood of Jesus. I was washed, I was sanctified, I was justified in the name of the Lord Jesus and by the Spirit of my God. I will flee sexual immorality and I will flee idolatry, and when temptation comes I will look for the way of escape that You, the faithful God, have already made. I declare that my freedom is for love. I will not use my knowledge to inflate myself or my liberty to wound my brother for whom Christ died. Like Paul, I will lay down my rights so that I might win some. Whatever I eat, whatever I drink, whatever I do, I will do it to the glory of God. I declare that I am a member of the body of Christ. I will not say, ‘I don’t belong,’ and I will not say to any member, ‘I have no need of you.’ I will honour the hidden members, suffer with those who suffer and rejoice with those who are honoured. I will use the gift You gave me for the profit of all. And above every gift I will pursue love — love that is patient and kind, that does not envy or boast, that keeps no record of wrongs, that bears, believes, hopes and endures all things, and that never fails. I declare that Christ died for my sins according to the Scriptures, that He was buried, and that He was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures. He is the first fruits, and I am part of His harvest. One day, in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet, I will be changed. Death, where is your sting? Hades, where is your victory? Thanks be to God, who gives me the victory through my Lord Jesus Christ! Therefore I will be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, because I know that my labour is not in vain in You. I will watch, I will stand firm in the faith, I will be courageous and strong — and I will let all that I do be done in love. Maranatha! Come, Lord Jesus. In the mighty name of Jesus, Amen!”
